Vallejo acrylics adhere well to photo-etched parts; priming with a metal or Vallejo primer strengthens the bond
Photo-etching uses a photo-sensitive material to create intricate details on a metal sheet; resulting parts are thin, flexible, and can be bent to fit curved surfaces
PE workspace should be well-lit with a clean, flat surface; a magnifying glass or lamp helps see small parts
Carefully cut PE parts from the fret with scissors or hobby knife; parts are fragile so be gentle
Clean PE parts with a soft brush or cotton swab to remove excess etch or debris
Bend PE parts with a PE bending tool or gently with tweezers for smaller parts
Attach PE parts with a small amount of super glue or cyanoacrylate, holding in place for a few seconds to set
Use a hobby knife or sanding stick to remove excess glue or etch that squeezed out during attachment
Vallejo acrylics offer excellent coverage with minimal buildup, consistent color and texture, and durable chip-resistant finish once cured
Use a fine brush (0/0 or 1/0), thin paint with Vallejo thinner or water, work in thin coats, and avoid over-handling PE parts since skin oil affects adhesion
When masking PE parts use a gentle touch and high-quality masking material such as Tamiya masking tape or liquid mask
Gator's Grip is an acrylic-based adhesive for small PE parts; dries clear and doesn't fog or yellow over time
Tacky Wax is a gentle, non-toxic adhesive wax for attaching small parts; holds securely without damaging surrounding area
Micro-Mark's Micro-Set is a low-viscosity adhesive for small PE parts; dries clear and doesn't fog or yellow over time
Two-part epoxies like JB Weld or Devcon suit larger PE parts needing a strong bond
Follow manufacturer instructions, use small amounts of adhesive, hold part until set, and test on an inconspicuous area first; alternatives may take longer to set than super glue
Cut wire to desired length, remove insulation or coating with wire strippers or sandpaper, and clean with a soft brush or cloth
Use round-nose pliers or curved-jaw wire bender for curved shapes, flat-nose pliers for sharp bends; work in small sections to avoid kinking
Create a jig or template from plastic, wood, or metal to reproduce consistent bends and shapes multiple times
Anneal stiff or brittle wire by heating with a hairdryer or torch until pliable; relieves stresses and eases bending
Use a soldering station with temperature control and stand; work in a well-ventilated area to avoid inhaling solder and flux fumes
For engine wiring and fuel lines twist multiple wires into bundles, solder at regular intervals, add small solder blobs to simulate connections, then paint and weather
Study reference photos to plan wire bundle route along engine and chassis contours; secure with wire clips and wire ties, then blend with paint and weathering
Study reference photos and consult Camaro enthusiasts for accuracy; keep wire detailing subtle to avoid detracting from overall appearance
